questions.question: What are you working on now?
questions.answer: I'm a full-stack developer on Doppket, a digital-asset marketplace at Dost11, MBC's AI strategy subsidiary. I've owned Korean-market localization, the product dashboard, the blog CMS, and the checkout UX, and I led onboarding for our first B2B client. I turned a photobooth feature I pitched in a meeting into a prototype in three days, and I redesigned the UI/UX of a broadcast CG compositing tool side by side with ML researchers in a shared repo.

questions.question: What matters most to you when collaborating?
questions.answer: What I value most is everyone on the team calling the same thing by the same name. Mismatched terms are where misunderstandings and bugs begin, so wherever I've worked I've aligned the vocabulary first. At Dost11 I proposed bringing everything to one standard, from screen labels to error messages across some 50 backend files, and did the cleanup myself. Like a librarian who first pins down what someone is actually looking for, I think collaboration starts there too. The quality a machine can catch, I leave to automation — PR-first work with ESLint, Prettier, and Git hooks — so people can spend their energy on what actually needs agreement. So I don't just propose and leave it; I see it through, and I document both what I'm handing off and what I decided not to fix, with the reasons, so the next person can pick it up right away. Being transparent even about what I didn't do is where trust on a team comes from.

questions.question: How do you use AI tools?
questions.answer: Heavily, especially to work through and pressure-test my own thinking. I keep a config that injects my personal and work code style and working rules into Claude Code, so I get consistent results across machines. When Claude Code first launched I was at Chainshift, and though D3.js was new to me, AI sped me up enough to finish the dashboard and support the sales demo. It also works in reverse: on a hiring assignment I replaced AI-generated code with code I wrote myself to unify error handling, documented it in an analysis doc, and landed the offer. Lately I've been working with AI inside products too, like a few-shot font-generation pipeline and an ML monorepo.

questions.question: How does your SQA/CX background help in frontend work?
questions.answer: Great UX is bug-free, and great UI is consistent. That's a principle from my QA and CX years. Doing SQA and CX at two companies, I saw first-hand where users get confused and drop off, and it still shapes how I write code. I split errors into the predictable (400/422) and the unpredictable (5xx/network) and handle each by policy, and I apply performance strategies like virtualization against numeric thresholds, kicking in at 50 items. Setting up issue trackers, unifying terminology, and building design systems are habits I picked up back then too.

questions.question: Why did you move into development?
questions.answer: I majored in Library & Information Science and worked on a people database at Yonhap News, then in QA and CX at a logistics startup and at Fitogether. I cut a response form down to a single page, raised the opt-in profile submission rate by 30%, and lowered communication costs with a shared glossary. That's where it clicked for me: what I enjoy is shaping information so it's easy for people to use. But in QA and CX I could only propose improvements and hand them off, and I kept wanting to build and fix things myself. I'd been coding since 2020, so moving into development felt natural.

questions.question: You're not a CS major — how did you build your fundamentals?
questions.answer: Library & Information Science is the study of classifying and structuring information, so my instinct for data modeling and consistent terminology actually comes from my major. I started coding there too, through courses like Information Technology (Python) and Software Programming, and I fill the gaps by building things myself. I implemented a TrueType font writer from scratch in pure Swift and published shared components as an npm library (formkit-react). My quality-engineering theory is backed by the ISTQB and CSTS certifications.

formkit.title: formkit-react
formkit.lead: A React form library I built and published to npm.
formkit.description: I refined the form-building lessons from Codeit Sprint projects like albaform into patterns while doing a hiring assignment, then grew the result into a library. I designed a composable API with the Compound Component pattern and packed Zod validation, accessibility (ARIA), and TypeScript types into a single package. Built with Vite, verified with GitHub Actions, then published.

albaform.title: albaform
albaform.lead: A part-time job marketplace built by a team.
albaform.description: I split SSR (for search visibility) from CSR (for interaction) and isolated global config to preserve SSR, reaching Google Lighthouse SEO 100. I branched permissions and rendering across six user states to block unauthorized access, unified screens with shared components, and sped up responsiveness with optimistic updates.

openmind.title: OpenMind
openmind.lead: An anonymous Q&A service built as a Codeit team project.
openmind.description: I implemented infinite scroll with IntersectionObserver and an isHydrated guard, eliminating the duplicate and missed API requests that came from depending on render timing. The observer disconnects immediately at the end of the list, and data loads without errors even in edge cases like an empty feed, back navigation, and URL changes. Built with JavaScript, React, CSS Modules, Axios, and Storybook.
openmind.alt: OpenMind anonymous question service landing screen

tappytype.title: TappyType
tappytype.lead: An iOS app that turns Apple Pencil handwriting into a Korean font.
tappytype.description: I built the app with Swift, SwiftUI, and PencilKit and took it solo all the way to launch. I separated the app and server behind a REST contract so swapping the model never touches app code, and since launch I've kept shipping updates solo — multi-project (1.1), notebook input, and pen presets (1.5).

portfolio.title: Portfolio site
portfolio.lead: The very site you're looking at.
portfolio.description: A timeline design that shows career, projects, and education alongside a generative-AI history, with a Pochacco cursor companion that follows your mouse. Built with Next.js App Router and TypeScript, with shared components and automation (ESLint, Prettier, Husky) keeping the code style consistent. The résumé (HTML and PDF) lives in this same repo: facts like dates and metrics sit in a single source of truth, both documents regenerate with one command, and tests fail if the site and résumé drift apart.

bodycodi.title: bodycodi
bodycodi.lead: A take-home assignment where I investigated the company's JSP legacy first-hand, inferred and defined coexistence constraints, and designed for gradual integration.
bodycodi.description: It includes a tw- prefix convention doc, central error handling that distinguishes predictable from unpredictable failures, conditional virtualization above a 50-item threshold (smooth scrolling even at 7,000), and a test control panel that lets the reviewer change data size and network latency to verify. The code is private — happy to share on request.
bodycodi.alt: bodycodi take-home assignment intro card (JSP legacy coexistence design)

nexca.title: Nexca console — frontend refactor
nexca.lead: At Chainshift I cleaned up the frontend architecture of a SaaS usage-management console.
nexca.description: I replaced 15 pass-through Next.js API routes with a single catch-all proxy, and unified the per-screen form and error handling with a react-hook-form-based shared Form component (compound pattern) and one HTTP-status-based error handler. The code is private — happy to share on request.

dotfiles.title: Claude Code config (dotfiles)
dotfiles.lead: The public edition of my real Claude Code setup, with sensitive parts removed.
dotfiles.description: I organized 30 React and 13 Python style rules into skills, and used CLAUDE.md to enforce reading the relevant rules before editing any .tsx or .py file. The rules are patterns that solidified in real projects like formkit-react and albaform, so code and guide validate each other. The config directory itself is a git repo, and launchd pulls hourly then auto-commits and pushes changes, so I work with the same rules on any machine.

seo-talk.title: SEO lightning talk
seo-talk.description: A lightning talk that defines a search engine as 'a product that gives information seekers the value of having their information needs met,' grouping 40-some SEO techniques under web standards, speed, and reliability. Starting backward from a search engine developer's concerns — crawl budget, server cost, accessibility — reveals the reason behind each ranking criterion, and the same principles carry into GEO in the LLM era (Bing indexing, easy-to-cite structure).
seo-talk.alt: Slide grouping 40-some SEO techniques into three branches: web standards, speed, reliability

cx-talk.title: The developer as service worker — lightning talk
cx-talk.description: A lightning talk at a Dost11 dev meeting titled 'CX 101 for thoughtful development.' Through the lens of a server response as a service interaction, it contrasts three responses customers react negatively to (causing harm, ignoring context, amateur handling) with a librarian's reference service (defining together what's being sought and guiding step by step). The core point: a good error message is itself DX and marketing.
cx-talk.alt: Slide expressing the USER–SERVICE relationship: 'the service offers an experience first, and I respond to it'

settlement.title: Settlement feature design
settlement.lead: A record of designing Korea-style monthly settlement on top of a foreign payment engine and handing it off to the team.
settlement.description: I organized design decisions — monthly close and snapshots, a state machine with locking, idempotency, sensitive-data boundaries — and the settlement UI and price snapshots I built myself into insights, example code, and concept diagrams. Internal company details are generalized.
settlement.alt: Settlement feature design case study page

aicg.title: Broadcast CG compositing tool — Gradio UI/UX redesign
aicg.lead: Sharing one repo with ML researchers, I redesigned the frontend of a broadcast CG compositing tool.
aicg.description: The tool was Gradio, but the essence was the same: translating the user's workflow into screen structure. I restructured tool-named English tabs into the actual work order — 1. Mask → 2. Asset → 3. Composite — and added an 'original + mask + asset = composite' thumbnail timeline so the screen shows where each output feeds next. I also handled Korean UI terminology and broadcast-grade 5GB uploads.
